digest.top_line: ASTRO brain mets guideline: SRS strongly recommended for up to 4 intact mets (ECOG 0-2), conditionally for 5-10; size-tiered SRS dose grid and HA-WBRT plus memantine codified.
digest.tldr: A guideline-and-consensus day, no new outcome data. ASTRO (CNS) and ESTRO (spine) codify SRS/SBRT dose by lesion size and BED10, with 2x12Gy conditionally preferred for painful spine mets. Sacral SBRT contouring and pelvic SABR re-RT consensus both left gaps: CTV kappa 0.59, and no agreement on cumulative OAR limits or re-RT interval.

sites.intro: Spine SBRT gets an ESTRO dose and technique framework (above 1x18Gy equivalent, PTV margin ≤3mm) plus the first sacrum-specific contouring consensus.

studies.name: International consensus: target volume delineation for sacral metastases and spinal SBRT
studies.tldr: CTV kappa 0.59 vs GTV 0.73 across 9 experts contouring 10 sacral metastasis cases; compartment-based CTV rules and an eight-segment sacral map proposed.
details: 🔍 9 experts (8 RO, 1 neurosurgeon) from 9 international centres contoured GTV, CTV and neural elements on 10 sacral metastasis cases
🔍 Panel experience: >7850 spine SBRT cases, median 13 yrs (range 7-18) treating spine SBRT
🔍 Agreement by STAPLE at an 80% confidence level, kappa corrected for chance agreement
📊 GTV kappa 0.73 (range 0.59-0.83), substantial agreement
📊 CTV kappa 0.59 (range 0.41-0.70), moderate agreement
⚠️ Lowest CTV agreement: Case 2 (kappa = 0.41) and Case 4 (kappa = 0.48), ala disease encroaching on VB and posterior elements

rows: Whole GTV compartment plus adjacent compartment(s), or at least 3 to 5 mm into adjacent bone

details: 📊 Modified STAPLE CTV accepted by consensus in 9 of 10 cases; Case 5 predominant only (6 of 9, 67%)

details.text: 🔍 Key CTV rules stated in text
subdetails: Include the whole involved compartment plus the adjacent marrow space at risk
GTV in any part of the S1 ala: CTV starts at the superior S1 ala
Uninvolved ala included prophylactically: visible ossification line may limit CTV size
Involved ala: ossification line is not a barrier, do not trim CTV to it
Thecal sac contoured to inferior S5 VB as cauda equina surrogate

details: 🔍 New sacral classification system: 8 segments (VB, left/right anterior and posterior ala, left/right lamina, spinous process)
⚠️ Bone-confined disease only; epidural or paraspinal extension, re-irradiation and postoperative sacrum not addressed
⚠️ No sacrum-specific pattern-of-failure data behind the rules; no external validation
🔗 Extends the Cox et al. and Redmond et al. mobile-spine contouring guidelines, which did not cover the sacrum

verdict.rationale: Expert contouring consensus from 10 cases and 9 experts; agreement measures panel coherence, not outcomes. No sacral pattern-of-failure or external validation.
verdict.audience: Sacral metastases confined to bone, SBRT candidates

studies.significance: The rule that changes contours is the S1 ala exception: any GTV in the S1 ala starts the CTV above the S1 VB, and an involved ala's ossification line is not a barrier. Disagreement concentrated at ala lesions abutting posterior elements (CTV kappa 0.41, 0.48), so that boundary stays physician judgment.
studies.monday_clinic: In bone-confined sacral metastases planned for SBRT, this gives a compartment-based CTV template keyed to the sacral classification system; it does not extend to epidural or paraspinal extension, re-irradiation, or the postoperative sacrum.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International expert contouring exercise: **8 radiation oncologists and 1 neurosurgeon** from 9 academic centres independently contoured GTV, CTV and neural elements on **10 sacral metastasis cases** previously treated with SBRT. Agreement by STAPLE at 80% confidence with kappa statistics; acceptance of the modified consensus contour voted per case (consensus defined as >75% of experts).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Cases chosen to represent a range of tumour sizes and locations across S1 to S5, from midline VB lesions to ala disease with foraminal or epidural extension. Planning CT fused with T1, T2 and T1 post-gadolinium MRI per SPINO guidelines.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Compartmental CTV**: the involved compartment plus adjacent marrow at risk, mapped to an eight-segment sacral classification system. **S1 ala exception**: any S1 ala GTV starts the CTV at the superior S1 ala. Thecal sac contoured to the **inferior S5 VB** as cauda equina surrogate; lumbosacral nerve roots per Yi et al., typically restricted to no hot spots.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **GTV kappa 0.73** (range 0.59-0.83), **CTV kappa 0.59** (range 0.41-0.70), P < .001 for all cases. Modified STAPLE CTV reached consensus acceptance in **9 of 10 cases**; Case 5 was predominant (6 of 9, 67%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Mirrors the compartmental logic of the Cox et al. (intact) and Redmond et al. (postoperative) mobile-spine guidelines, which left out the sacrum. A cited imaging-based sacral SBRT series reported cumulative LC **86.5% at 1 year and 78.7% at 2 years**, median time to local recurrence 4.7 months.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents sacral metastases confined to bone treated with de novo SBRT. Does not represent epidural or paraspinal extension, re-irradiation, or the postoperative sacrum.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Three experts preferred a **0-5 mm isotropic margin** over the compartmental approach, citing nerve root and bowel toxicity and sacral insufficiency fracture risk. Dose and fractionation are not specified in the main text, and OAR constraints sit in the supplement.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The sacral classification system is the durable product: it gives a common language for reporting sacral volumes and failures. Whether compartmental expansion improves sacral LC, or only adds toxicity, **remains untested**.

studies.interpretation:
This paper fills a defined gap. The mobile-spine consensus contours, Cox et al. for intact disease and Redmond et al. for the postoperative spine, left the sacrum out, and no sacrum-specific pattern-of-failure analysis exists. What it supplies is a vocabulary, the eight-segment sacral classification system, plus CTV rules derived from expert contours. It does not supply outcome data. Read it as a standardization instrument: its value lies less in whether each rule is optimal than in making sacral SBRT volumes reportable in a shared language, so that future failure analyses can be pooled across centres.

The agreement numbers carry a predictable shape. GTV agreement (kappa 0.73) exceeded CTV agreement (kappa 0.59), as expected when one volume is defined by imaging and the other encodes judgment about microscopic spread. The informative part is where agreement broke down. Cases 2 and 4, with kappas of 0.41 and 0.48, were ala lesions encroaching on the vertebral body and posterior elements. That is exactly where the compartmental approach pushes the CTV toward nerve roots and bowel, and it is where three experts preferred a 0 to 5 mm isotropic margin, citing nerve root and bowel toxicity and sacral insufficiency fracture. So the consensus is firmest for central vertebral body lesions, where the decision is easy, and weakest at the lateral and posterior boundary, where it matters.

The acceptance vote should also be weighed carefully. Consensus in 9 of 10 cases sounds decisive, but the panel voted on a contour derived from its own submissions. That shows the panel is internally coherent. It does not show that the contours are correct. Highly significant kappa p-values only establish that agreement beat chance, a low bar for nine experienced academic spine SBRT clinicians. The panel was also narrow: all academic, with dedicated spine SBRT programmes, and the 10 cases were selected for representativeness rather than accrued consecutively. The core anatomic argument, that the fused sacrum lacks the disc barrier thought to limit spread in the mobile spine, is plausible, but the authors call the supporting literature sparse. The S1 ala exception and the refusal to use an involved ala's ossification line as a boundary are reasoning from anatomy, not from failure data.

Scope is the biggest constraint on transfer. The rules cover bone-confined disease only, excluding epidural extension, paraspinal disease, re-irradiation and the postoperative sacrum. Yet the authors' own review of a sacral SBRT series describes bulkier disease at presentation, with progression in the vertebral body together with paraspinal tissue, followed by isolated epidural progression, as the dominant failure patterns. That series reported cumulative LC of 86.5% at 1 year and 78.7% at 2 years. The scenarios this guideline excludes may therefore account for much of the sacral failure burden, and the margins for them remain individual judgment.

The rules would be wrong if sacral failures turn out to be mainly epidural or paraspinal rather than marrow-contiguous. In that case, compartmental bony expansion would add plexopathy and fracture risk without improving local control. The classification system is what makes that question testable. The practical read is to adopt the nomenclature for reporting, use the CTV rules for bone-confined disease, and treat the ala and posterior-element boundary as unresolved.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The S1 ala exception changes contours: any GTV in the S1 ala starts the CTV above the S1 VB, and an involved ala's ossification line is not a barrier. CTV agreement was lowest for ala lesions abutting posterior elements (kappa 0.41, 0.48), so that boundary stays physician judgment.

open_questions: Sacrum-specific pattern of failure after SBRT
Sacral plexus and nerve root dose tolerance
CTV for epidural or paraspinal sacral extension

studies.tldr: 22 recommendations, 5 statements: spine SBRT dose above 1x18Gy (BED10=50Gy10) for LC; 2x12Gy conditionally preferred for painful mets; PTV margin ≤3mm.
details: 🔍 ESTRO guideline built on a PRISMA systematic review, Jan 2005-Sep 2021 (RTOG 0631 added Apr 2023)
🔍 22 recommendations + 5 statements; consensus threshold ≥75% panel agreement

subdetails: Prescription above 1x18Gy equivalent (BED10=50Gy10) for durable LC
De novo high-dose schedules: 1x20Gy, 1x24Gy, 2x12Gy, 3x10Gy, 5x7Gy; expected LC 80-90% at 1-2y
2x12Gy conditionally recommended as preferred palliative SBRT schedule
16 or 18Gy x1 not recommended over 1x8Gy when pain relief or QoL is the goal
Not frankly unstable (SINS >12 excluded)
Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous vertebral segments in the volume

GTV/CTV to PTV margin ≤3mm, minimum PTV margin 1mm
Intensity-modulated delivery; online IGRT before each fraction
Cord PRV prioritized over target coverage

Single-fraction >20Gy: increased VCF vs CRT and vs fractionated SBRT

subdetails: VCF 6-14% in two large multicenter analyses
Myelopathy 0.4% in pooled analysis of >1,000 de novo pts

⚠️ Re-irradiation and symptomatic MSCC excluded from scope

verdict.rationale: ESTRO practice guideline from a PRISMA systematic review with ≥75% panel consensus; most recommendations rest on moderate or expert-opinion evidence, not new outcome data.

studies.significance: The dose floor is the actionable line: above 1x18Gy (BED10=50Gy10), with 2x12Gy preferred for painful mets, because RTOG 0631's 16 or 18Gy single fraction lost to 8Gy on 3mo pain response (41.3% vs 60.5%). Single fractions >20Gy carry high-level VCF evidence, so 24Gy x1 for oligomets trades LC against fracture.
studies.monday_clinic: In an unirradiated painful spine met that is not frankly unstable, Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous segments, with prolonged life expectancy, this supports considering SBRT over conventional RT; it does not extend to symptomatic MSCC, re-irradiation, or short life expectancy, where conventional RT stays preferred.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO clinical practice guideline built on a PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Embase and Cochrane (Jan 2005-Sep 2021), with RTOG 0631 added Apr 2023. ASTRO methodology graded evidence and recommendation strength; **≥75% agreement** defined consensus.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Vertebral metastases from solid malignancies, painful or oligometastatic, previously unirradiated. **Re-irradiation and symptomatic MSCC excluded** from scope.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Dose above 1x18Gy (BED10=50Gy10)** for durable LC; **2x12Gy conditionally preferred** palliative schedule. PTV margin ≤3mm (minimum 1mm), intensity-modulated delivery, daily IGRT, cord PRV prioritized over coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: VCF is the most frequent AE (6-14% in two multicenter analyses); **single fractions >20Gy raise VCF risk** (high-level evidence). Myelopathy 0.4% in a pooled de novo series of >1,000 pts; routine prophylactic steroids for pain flare **not recommended**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The pain recommendation leans on **SC.24** (24Gy/2fx vs 20Gy/5fx: CR 35% vs 14%, p=0.0002). **RTOG 0631** (16 or 18Gy x1 vs 8Gy x1) showed no pain gain, which the panel reads as a dose-floor problem rather than a failure of technique.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents unirradiated spine mets that are not frankly unstable, Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous segments, with prolonged life expectancy. Does not represent re-irradiation, symptomatic MSCC, or short life expectancy where conventional RT is preferred.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Search closed Sep 2021 apart from RTOG 0631; ROBOMET is abstract-only and the TwiCs trial was underpowered with non-standardized dosing. Panel is radonc-weighted with one spine surgeon and no medical oncologist, yet addresses concurrent targeted/IO toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Dose, not technique, organizes the document: low single-fraction SBRT matched or trailed 8Gy, while higher doses improved CR and LC at a fracture cost. 2-5 fraction schedules are the hedge where fracture management capacity is limited.

studies.interpretation:
The guideline's center of gravity is a dose argument, and the randomized data under it are less uniform than the recommendations read. SC.24 carries the pain recommendation: 24Gy in 2 fractions beat 20Gy in 5 on 3-month complete response (35% vs 14%), and the Sunnybrook subcohort extended the advantage into local failure and re-irradiation. RTOG 0631, the largest trial, went the other way, with 16 or 18Gy single-fraction SBRT showing no pain improvement over 8Gy and a higher response rate with conventional RT. The panel reconciles the two by dose rather than by technique, which is why the floor sits above 1x18Gy and why 16 or 18Gy single fraction is explicitly not recommended as a replacement for 8Gy when pain relief is the goal. That reading is coherent, but it is an inference across trials with different populations, pain definitions and fractionation, not a head-to-head dose comparison.

The oligometastatic case is thinner. The 80-95% LC at 1-2 years from the systematic review is drawn largely from non-randomized series, and the one randomized dose comparison cited (24Gy single fraction vs 27Gy in 3 fractions, 117 pts, 56% spinal) favored the higher single dose for local control. The guideline sets that directly against its fracture statements: single fractions above 20Gy carry a high-level association with VCF versus both CRT and fractionated SBRT, while fractionated SBRT does not raise fracture risk over CRT. The consequence is a choice the document deliberately leaves to institutions. 24Gy in 1 fraction buys local control at a fracture cost, and 2 to 5 fraction schedules are the hedge for centers less able to manage fractures.

Selection criteria do much of the work and deserve more weight than the dose tables. Only 2% of SC.24 SBRT pts had high-grade epidural disease, and RTOG 0631 mandated a 3mm cord gap. The recommended population (not frankly unstable, Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous segments, prolonged life expectancy) mirrors who was actually studied, and the guideline states plainly that conventional RT remains preferred for short life expectancy, inability to tolerate MRI or immobilization, or pain too severe to wait for MR-based planning. Separation surgery followed by SBRT is described as an emerging trend, not endorsed broadly, which is the appropriate weight given no randomized data were cited for it.

The technical recommendations (MRI-based delineation, ≤1.5mm simulation slices, PTV margin ≤3mm with a 1mm minimum, cord PRV prioritized over coverage, daily image guidance) are framed as the conditions under which the existing evidence base should reproduce, including technology the trials predate. Their value is in drawing a boundary: a center that cannot hold an end-to-end tolerance under 2mm sits outside that evidence base whatever dose it prescribes.

What the document cannot settle is whether 2x12Gy, the conditionally preferred palliative schedule, transfers beyond the high-volume programs that generated SC.24, and how SBRT interacts with concurrent targeted therapy or immunotherapy, where the recommendation is only to discuss the risk with the treating medical oncologist. Re-irradiation and symptomatic MSCC, two of the harder spine decisions in practice, are outside its scope entirely.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dose floor is the actionable line: above 1x18Gy (BED10=50Gy10), with 2x12Gy preferred for painful mets, because RTOG 0631's 16 or 18Gy single fraction trailed 8Gy on 3mo pain response (41.3% vs 60.5%). Single fractions >20Gy carry high-level VCF evidence, so 24Gy x1 for oligomets trades LC against fracture.

open_questions: Does 2x12Gy transfer beyond high-volume SC.24-type centers?
Spine SBRT safety with concurrent targeted therapy or immunotherapy
Role of separation surgery before SBRT in high-grade epidural disease

studies.name: International Delphi consensus: pelvic SABR re-irradiation
studies.tldr: 66% of statements reached consensus among 21-23 international radiation oncologists; interval since prior RT, lesion number/size and cumulative OAR limits stayed unresolved.
details: 🔍 3-round Delphi, 23 radiation oncologists in Round 1 (56% of 41 invited); 21 and 22 in Rounds 2-3
🔍 Panel weighted to GU: 19 (83%) GU, 11 (48%) lower GI, 8 (35%) gyn subspecialty interest
🔍 44 statements after Round 1; 29 reached consensus in Round 2, 15 re-presented in Round 3

details.text: 📊 Panel agreement on selected statements (values from the paper's text)

rows: SABR re-RT not usually appropriate with direct luminal OAR invasion
May not be appropriate with luminal OAR contact (no invasion)
Minimum 12 mo since prior pelvic RT
PTV point max dose not to exceed 140%

subdetails: Alternative to surgical exenteration after MDT discussion
May be considered with extra-pelvic oligometastatic disease controllable by MDT
Feasibility weighs lesion number, target size, location and OAR proximity
Minimum WHO PS 2 (or equivalent)
Expected/transient prior acute RT toxicity does not in itself preclude re-RT

details: 📐 Agreed fractionation: 30-37.5 Gy in 5-6 fx or 21-27 Gy in 3 fx, alternate days
📐 Delivery agreement: IMRT (or similar high-conformity) plus daily online volumetric or fiducial verification
⚠️ Proposed cumulative OAR constraints (AAPM TG-101 5-fx limits used cumulatively) did not reach consensus
⚠️ Agreement measures expert opinion; no control or toxicity outcomes were generated by this study

verdict.rationale: Delphi panel output: agreement percentages measure expert opinion, not outcomes. Frames practice where no randomised re-irradiation data exist; key dosimetric questions explicitly unresolved.
verdict.audience: Pelvic recurrence after prior pelvic RT, SABR re-irradiation candidates

studies.significance: The transferable piece is the agreed technique: 30-37.5 Gy in 5-6 fx or 21-27 Gy in 3 fx on alternate days, IMRT, daily volumetric verification. Luminal OAR contact split the panel at 50% while direct invasion was a 90% exclusion, so contact cases remain judgment calls without a consensus fallback.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with pelvic recurrence after prior pelvic RT, no direct luminal OAR invasion, and WHO PS 2 or better, this supports SABR re-irradiation as an MDT option alongside exenteration; it does not settle the interval since prior RT or cumulative OAR limits.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Three-round **international Delphi**; Round 1 opened 27/10/2020, Round 3 closed 22/03/2021. 44 statements after Round 1, **29 reached consensus in Round 2**, 15 re-presented in Round 3.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel of radiation/clinical oncologists who had published on pelvic SABR re-irradiation or were judged international experts; one per research group. **23 of 41 invited** joined Round 1; median 10 cases/yr per participant (range 10-100). Subspecialty interest **GU 19 (83%)**, lower GI 11 (48%), gyn 8 (35%).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Agreed schedules: **30-37.5 Gy in 5-6 fx or 21-27 Gy in 3 fx**, alternate days. Agreement also covered IMRT-level conformity and **daily online volumetric or fiducial verification**. The 140% PTV point-max cap reached only 73%; 1 participant favoured 115-125%.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **66% of statements reached consensus**, covering definition, patient selection, set-up, delineation, planning and delivery. **No consensus** on minimum interval since prior RT (43% for 12 mo), maximum lesion number/size, or cumulative OAR constraints.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Sits beside the ESTRO ACROP Delphi on salvage SBRT for intraprostatic relapse, which addresses a narrower prostate-only scenario. A thoracic re-irradiation Delphi hit the same wall: no agreed quantified dose overlap to define re-irradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SABR re-irradiation of pelvic recurrence after prior pelvic RT, with an MDT and an experienced physics/RTT team. Does not represent conventionally fractionated or hyperfractionated pelvic re-irradiation, or cases with direct luminal OAR invasion.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The panel is **GU-dominant**, so transfer to gyn and rectal recurrences rests on fewer voices. Optimal OAR constraints were borrowed from **de novo AAPM TG-101 limits used cumulatively**, not from re-irradiation outcome data.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The selection and technique framework is usable now. The unresolved items (interval, lesion count/size, cumulative constraints with recovery) are the ones that set the dose actually deliverable, so the core dosimetric decision remains **case-by-case**.

studies.interpretation:
This document is most useful where it agrees and most informative where it does not. The areas of agreement are largely procedural: who belongs in the MDT, how to immobilise and prepare bladder and rectum, which imaging to fuse, which OARs to contour, and that IMRT-level conformity and daily volumetric verification are expected. Almost nobody practicing pelvic SABR re-irradiation would argue with any of that, and the high agreement reflects how uncontroversial it is. The agreed fractionation range, 30-37.5 Gy in 5-6 fractions or 21-27 Gy in 3 fractions on alternate days, is the closest the paper comes to a dosimetric anchor, and it gives departments a defensible default to point to.

The failures to agree carry more information. The panel could not settle a minimum interval since prior RT (43% backed 12 months), a cap on lesion number or size, or cumulative OAR constraints. Those are exactly the parameters that decide whether a meaningful re-irradiation dose can be delivered at all. The comments on the interval statement are telling: several participants argued that previously delivered OAR dose and primary disease type matter more than elapsed time, which amounts to saying the question is posed on the wrong axis. Similarly, direct luminal OAR invasion drew 90% agreement as a contraindication, yet contact without invasion split the panel at 50%, with lower total dose, compromised PTV coverage, or close intra/inter-fraction monitoring offered as workarounds. Contact is the common clinical scenario, so the gap sits where the reader most needs guidance.

The constraint problem reflects the evidence base. The proposed optimal constraints were the AAPM TG-101 de novo 5-fraction limits applied cumulatively, and the less conservative published approaches cited in Table 4 come from small retrospective series: Abusaris et al reported no grade 3+ toxicity at median 15 months follow-up, and Smith et al one grade 3 pain event at median 24.5 months. Short follow-up in re-irradiated bowel and sacral plexus is precisely where late events would hide, so the reluctance to endorse higher cumulative limits with assumed tissue recovery is defensible rather than timid.

Panel composition should temper how a reader applies this outside prostate. Most participants listed a GU interest, fewer lower GI, fewer still gyn, and the organisers were UK-based. A gyn reader facing a sidewall recurrence after prior brachytherapy is working in territory the panel covered thinly, and the brachytherapy overlap statement did not settle either. Response was also modest, with 23 of 41 invited joining Round 1, so the panel is a self-selected subset of an already selected expert pool.

What would make this obsolete is prospective outcome data with recorded cumulative OAR doses, which the panel itself endorsed collecting. Until then, the practical read is that the technique framework and patient-selection gates are a reasonable floor, and the cumulative constraint and interval decisions remain a per-case dosimetric judgment that no consensus currently backs.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The agreed technique is the transferable piece: 30-37.5 Gy in 5-6 fx or 21-27 Gy in 3 fx on alternate days, IMRT, daily volumetric verification. Luminal OAR contact split the panel at 50% versus a 90% exclusion for direct invasion, leaving contact cases without consensus backing.

open_questions: Minimum safe interval between pelvic RT courses
Cumulative OAR EQD2 limits allowing for tissue recovery
Maximum lesion number and size for pelvic SABR re-irradiation

📐 BED10 ≥5000 cGy associated with improved LC in a multi-institutional retrospective analysis
🔗 5-10 met rec rests on JLGK0901: noninferior post-SRS survival vs 2-4 mets, cumulative volume ≤15 cm3
⚠️ No randomized or prospective controlled data on SRS dose or fractionation
⚠️ NCT01592968 (SRS vs WBRT, 5-15 intact mets) final report unpublished at guideline development
🔍 SRS alone requires MRI every 2-3 mo for 1-2 yr, then every 4-6 mo

verdict.rationale: Society guideline graded by modified Delphi over an AHRQ review; no new outcome data. Dose-fractionation and 5-10 met SRS rows rest on Low QoE.

studies.significance: The dose grid is the RT payload: SF 2000-2400 cGy for <2 cm (Strong), SF 1800 cGy or 2700/3 or 3000/5 for ≥2 to <3 cm, multifraction for ≥3 to 4 cm. No randomized fractionation data exist, so thresholds rest on RTOG 90-05 MTDs and a BED10 ≥5000 cGy retrospective association.
studies.monday_clinic: In ECOG 0-2 pts with 5-10 intact brain mets, this conditionally supports SRS alone over WBRT; it does not extend to 11 to 15 mets, where the panel withheld a recommendation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASTRO task force guideline addressing **4 key questions**, built on an AHRQ systematic review of **97 studies**. Consensus by modified Delphi: **≥75%** agreement threshold (**≥90%** for expert opinion recommendations).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intact and resected brain metastases from nonhematologic solid tumors** in adults. Small cell lung cancer excluded from the KQ1 RCT evidence base.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SF SRS **2000-2400 cGy** for <2 cm; SF **1800 cGy** or MF **2700 cGy/3 fx** or **3000 cGy/5 fx** for ≥2 to <3 cm; **multifraction** for ≥3 to 4 cm. WBRT example **3000 cGy in 10 fractions**, with **hippocampal avoidance** for favorable prognosis.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Outcomes weighed: intracranial control, PFS, OS, neurocognitive function and patient-reported outcomes; **symptomatic radionecrosis** for KQ4.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: SRS-alone rows rest on five RCTs of local therapy with or without WBRT in 1 to 3 mets (one allowing 4), where WBRT improved intracranial control without a survival gain; **N0574** showed worse neurocognition and QoL with SRS plus WBRT. The 5-10 row rests on **JLGK0901**, an observational count-stratum comparison, not a WBRT comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ECOG 0-2 pts with intact or resected brain mets from nonhematologic solid tumors. Does not represent pts with 11 to 15 mets, mets >6 cm, or hematologic malignancies.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Literature cutoff **Sept 2020** predates NCT01592968, CCTG CE.7 and the DFCI SRS vs HA-WBRT plus memantine trials. The panel overrode AHRQ conclusions it deemed incongruent with practice by adding neurocognitive and QoL outcomes AHRQ had excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Deferral of local therapy for asymptomatic pts on CNS-active systemic therapy has **no randomized evidence**; cited response rates of approximately 30% to 75% come from trials that largely excluded symptomatic or steroid-requiring pts, and up to 40% show early progression without response.

studies.interpretation:
The core of this guideline is a reweighting of the WBRT question around neurocognition rather than survival. Its anchor is a set of five RCTs of local therapy with or without WBRT, all in 1 to 3 brain mets (one allowing 4), in which adding WBRT improved intracranial control without improving survival, with N0574 showing worse neurocognitive deterioration and QoL from the combination. That evidence is consistent and long-standing, which is why SRS for up to 4 intact mets carries the only Strong/High grade in KQ1. Nothing here challenges it; the guideline codifies a decade of drift away from WBRT.

The more consequential content sits in the rows with weaker grading. Extending SRS to 5-10 intact mets rests on JLGK0901, a prospective observational study comparing count strata within an SRS-treated cohort, not a randomized comparison against WBRT, plus retrospective survival data. The panel was disciplined about the boundary: it declined to extend the recommendation to 11 to 15 mets because only 10 pts in the supporting retrospective series fell in that band, and it flagged a Japanese series suggesting the worse survival seen with 5 to 15 mets might be driven by the highest-count subgroup. The conditional grade is honest. A reader treating a pt in the 5-10 band with SRS is inside the guideline but on a Low-quality evidence base, and the randomized answer, NCT01592968 comparing SRS with WBRT in 5 to 15 mets, was not available to the panel.

The dose-fractionation grid deserves the most skepticism from an RT reader. The guideline itself states that no randomized or prospective controlled study has compared clinical outcomes by SRS dose and fractionation. The size thresholds descend from RTOG 90-05, a phase 1 MTD study in pts previously treated with focal RT or WBRT, and the multifraction preference above 2 cm comes from retrospective series and a BED10 ≥5000 cGy association. These are sensible defaults rather than tested thresholds, and a lesion straddling a size cut next to the brainstem or optic apparatus remains a judgment call the grid does not resolve.

The systemic-therapy recommendations are expert-driven by necessity. There is no randomized evidence on upfront vs deferred RT for pts starting immunotherapy or CNS-active targeted agents, and the response data the panel cites come from trials that mostly excluded symptomatic or steroid-requiring pts and enrolled small-volume disease. Recommending upfront local therapy for symptomatic mets follows from that exclusion, not from a head-to-head result, and the deferral option for asymptomatic pts is appropriately conditional on surveillance access and salvage capacity.

What would make parts of this wrong: if CCTG CE.7 or the DFCI trial shows HA-WBRT plus memantine is neurocognitively comparable to SRS in higher-count disease, the 5-10 SRS row weakens. If prospective deferral data show early progression approaching the up-to-40% rate the panel cites, the asymptomatic deferral window narrows. The Sept 2020 literature cutoff means the guideline predates several trials it names as pending, and its own commitment to replacement or reaffirmation within 5 years of publication is the clock to watch.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The size-tiered SRS grid (SF 2000-2400 cGy <2 cm, SF 1800 cGy or 2700/3 or 3000/5 for ≥2 to <3 cm, multifraction ≥3 to 4 cm) and BED10 ≥5000 cGy anchor rest on phase 1 MTDs and retrospective data. SRS for 5-10 mets is conditional; HA plus memantine is the strongly recommended WBRT default.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Symptomatic brain mets get upfront local therapy before immunotherapy or CNS-active targeted agents (Strong). Deferral is a conditional MDT option only for asymptomatic pts, weighing size, location, number, expected CNS response and access to close surveillance and salvage.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Surgery is conditionally recommended for intact mets >4 cm, with neurosurgery discussion suggested for any lesion causing mass effect regardless of size. After resection, cavity SRS is strongly recommended to improve local control, making postoperative RT referral the default.

open_questions: SRS vs WBRT outcomes for 5-15 intact brain mets

studies.significance: The planning lever is bolus thickness, not the depth ceiling: at 5 mm depth on a 6×6 cm² CTV, going from 5 to 10 mm bolus cut skin Dmax 187% to 148% while R100-R50 widened 16.0 to 18.7 mm. With EQD2 at a 150% Dmax spanning 121.5 to 189 Gy across ACROP schedules, a flat percentage cap is a weak surface constraint.
studies.monday_clinic: In large NMSC infiltrating beyond 5 mm where interstitial BT or EBRT is not viable, this supports mould or flap BT with thicker or variable bolus to hold surface Dmax down; it does not extend to tumours suited to interstitial BT or EBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **PRISMA systematic review** by the GEC-ESTRO H&N and Skin Working Group, PubMed search through **31 May 2019**, plus a theoretical TG-43 planning exercise (Oncentra Brachy, Ir-192 HDR) on 6×6 and 10×10 cm² CTVs.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Clinical studies of **NMSC superficial HDR Ir-192 BT** with flaps or custom moulds; conference papers, surveys, case reports and reviews included, English only.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Planning model used parallel catheters at 1 cm spacing, 2 mm source step, prescription depths of 3, 5, 10 and 20 mm crossed with bolus of 3, 5, 10 and 20 mm. ACROP-listed mould/flap schedules range from 17-18 × 3 Gy to 8 × 5 Gy twice daily.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Thicker bolus **lowers surface Dmax at the cost of a shallower gradient**; the bolus × Dmax × R100-R50 trade is tabulated above for the 5 mm depth case.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: GEC-ESTRO ACROP, ABS, AAPM and GEB guidance converge on a **5 mm prescription ceiling** and ABS/GEB on **125% (flaps) / 140% (moulds)** surface Dmax. The ABS Dmax limit was modelled on its APBI consensus, where skin is an OAR rather than the target. Zaorsky's meta-analysis (EBRT 9965 vs BT 553 pts) favoured BT cosmesis but carried no bolus or Dmax data.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents large NMSC extending >5 mm below the skin surface where interstitial BT or EBRT is not an option. Does not represent standard thin lesions within current guideline limits or tumours suited to interstitial BT or EBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Dosimetry is TG-43 without scatter correction, with MC deviations up to 5% for flaps. Skin toxicity shows a volume and layer effect that a single surface Dmax point cannot capture, and telangiectasia needs **2-3 yr** follow-up to assess.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The 5 mm and 125-140% limits are **not tied to PROMs** in any published series, and deviating centres report similar results. The group calls for standardized dosimetry reporting and homogeneous multicentre data via the **COBRA** project before revising thresholds.

studies.interpretation:
The working group is not overturning the 5 mm prescription-depth ceiling so much as exposing what holds it up. The ACROP, ABS and GEB documents agree on that ceiling and on surface Dmax caps of 125% for flaps and 140% for moulds, yet the review finds no published series tying either figure to local control, toxicity or cosmesis. The caps read as inherited convention. The ABS skin Dmax limit followed the template of its APBI consensus, where skin is an organ at risk sitting over a deeper target. In NMSC the skin is the target, so a tight surface cap risks underdosing tumour rather than protecting normal tissue.

The planning exercise is the part a physicist and radiation oncologist can use tomorrow. On a theoretical 6×6 cm² CTV prescribed at 5 mm, replacing the standard 5 mm bolus with 10 mm drops surface Dmax from 187% to 148%, while the 100% to 50% isodose separation widens from 16.0 to 18.7 mm. That is the bargain IMRT strikes against conformal RT: a cooler surface bought with more low-dose spread. The model also shows that a textbook 5 mm bolus at 5 mm depth does not meet the 125%-140% caps, which raises the question of how often current limits are actually being met. These are TG-43 numbers without scatter correction, and the review cites deviations up to 5% against Monte Carlo for flaps, so the absolute percentages carry calculation error. The direction of the bolus effect is geometric, though, and should survive a model-based algorithm.

The clinical support for prescribing deeper is thin in a specific way. Series reporting depths of 9, 10, 15 or 20 mm describe good control and cosmesis, but none separates the deep-prescription pts or states what share of the cohort they were. A reader cannot tell whether the favourable outcomes belong to the deep cases or are carried by the shallow majority. Surveys showing 2 of 16 ABS centres working past 5 mm, and Canadian centres treating depth as only a relative contraindication, establish that the practice exists, not that it is safe. The fractionation argument compounds the problem: at a 150% hotspot, the ACROP mould and flap schedules map to EQD2 anywhere from 121.5 to 189 Gy, so one percentage cap does not describe one biological exposure.

What the position moves is narrow. For a large NMSC infiltrating beyond 5 mm where interstitial BT and EBRT are not options, surface BT with tailored or 3D-printed bolus becomes a defensible plan rather than an off-guideline one. The thin lesion within current limits is untouched, and no new Dmax number is licensed; the group explicitly declines to propose one. The real weight of this paper rests on COBRA producing homogeneous dosimetry linked to outcomes, because until then Dmax itself is unstable: none of the reviewed papers says how it was computed, and DVH bin and sample settings shift it. The position would be wrong if thick-bolus deep plans turn out to trade surface reactions for higher dose in the hypodermal layers, a shift the review itself flags and that a skin-surface point metric would never detect.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The planning lever is bolus thickness, not the depth ceiling: at 5 mm depth on a 6×6 cm² CTV, going from 5 to 10 mm bolus cut skin Dmax 187% to 148% while R100-R50 widened 16.0 to 18.7 mm. EQD2 at a 150% Dmax spanning 121.5 to 189 Gy across ACROP schedules makes a flat percentage cap a weak surface constraint.
